To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rectal EIBs is a promising biomarker for proximal neoplastic lesions in females.
we have developed and clinically validated a novel optical method for detecting early increases in blood flow in the distal colon that is associated with the presence of proximal neoplastic lesions.

we have shown that the use of a novel optical technique, polarization-gated spectroscopic fiber-optic probe (PGSPF) to measure oxyhemoglobin in the endoscoped normal rectal mucosa, improves the sensitivity and specificity of flexible sigmoidoscopy for the detection of colorectal neoplasia in both men and women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new, minimally invasive, and cost effective screening tool that would improve the performance of flexible sigmoidoscopy in women.
the development of a new, noninvasive method for detecting early neoplasia and the application of this technology for improving colorectal cancer screening.
developing a new, optical, and noninvasive approach to detect early colorectal cancer.

the use of a novel light scattering technique in the endoscoped normal rectal mucosa of women is a robust and sensitive method to predict the presence of proximal neoplastic lesions.
the combination of rectal EIBs and flexible sigmoidoscopy is an excellent screening tool for colorectal cancer in men.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we were able to show that the rectal mucosa in women with advanced neoplasms in the proximal colon had a robust increase in blood supply when compared with neoplasia free women.

the use of rectal EIBIS may allow the flexible sigmoidosocpy to be considered as an acceptable colorectal cancer screening option in women.
